title: Brent Tops $100 as China Halts Fuel Exports
content: Oil prices climbed over the week, with Brent crude pushing back above $100 a barrel as renewed US-Iran tensions and China's suspension of refined-fuel exports for October offset signs of recovering Middle Eastern supply. Brent rose 4.5% from $97.45 to $101.88 a barrel while West Texas Intermediate edged 0.9% higher from $89.50 to $90.31, keeping an inflationary impulse running through global bond and equity markets.
summary: Brent crude rose 4.5% back above $100 a barrel as China's October fuel-export halt and Middle East risk offset recovering supply.
context:
• Elevated crude has been a central driver of 2026's global bond sell-off, feeding inflation fears and bets on tighter policy.

• A conflict in the Middle East has kept a risk premium in oil even as Saudi export volumes have begun to recover.

• Weakness elsewhere in commodities — lithium carbonate and iron ore led the week's falls — points to softer industrial demand.
happened:
• Brent gained 4.5% over the week to $101.88 a barrel, moving back above the $100 mark.

• WTI rose 0.9% to $90.31, remaining below $100.

• China suspended refined-fuel exports for October while renewed US-Iran tensions added to supply-side risk.
implications:
• Sustained crude above $100 complicates the disinflation narrative that markets are leaning on for central-bank relief.

• A Chinese export halt tightens regional product markets and could lift refining margins.

• Any de-escalation in the Middle East or firmer Saudi flows would be the clearest trigger for prices to retreat.
importance:
• Oil is the swing factor behind the inflation angst driving long-end yields higher worldwide.

• Energy costs feed directly into headline inflation ahead of the Federal Reserve's late-October decision.

• Commodity divergence — firm crude against falling metals — signals a market worried about prices, not growth.

title: Gold Tumbles 3.5% in Sharpest Weekly Drop
content: Gold suffered a sharp weekly reversal, falling about $149 an ounce, or 3.5%, to around $4,170 as rising real yields and a firmer tone in risk assets drew money out of the metal. Silver, copper and natural gas also ended the week lower, with gold trading near $4,140 an ounce on Friday as the multi-year Treasury sell-off lifted the opportunity cost of holding non-yielding assets.
summary: Gold fell 3.5% on the week to around $4,170 an ounce as surging Treasury yields raised the cost of holding bullion.
context:
• Gold had rallied strongly through 2026 on geopolitical risk and central-bank buying, leaving it exposed to a pullback.

• Higher real yields make non-yielding bullion relatively less attractive, pressuring prices.

• A broad commodity retreat, led by lithium and iron ore, accompanied the move lower in precious metals.
happened:
• Gold fell roughly $149 an ounce, or 3.5%, over the week to around $4,170.

• The metal traded near $4,140 an ounce on Friday, down about 0.9% on the day.

• Silver, copper and natural gas also closed the week lower.
implications:
• Further increases in long-end yields would keep pressure on bullion in the near term.

• A renewed flight to safety from equities or geopolitics could quickly reverse the pullback.

• The scale of the drop tests whether 2026's gold bulls treat weakness as a buying opportunity.
importance:
• Gold's slide underlines how dominant the rates story has become across asset classes.

• The move is a gauge of positioning after a crowded, record-setting rally in the metal.

• Precious-metals weakness alongside firm oil highlights a market repricing real rates, not growth.

title: US Payrolls Miss Badly, Easing Fed Hike Bets
content: The US labour market faltered in September, with nonfarm payrolls rising just 29,000 against forecasts of about 84,000 and the unemployment rate ticking up to 4.2%. The downside surprise, combined with a 60,000 downward revision to July and August, pushed traders to price a far higher chance the Federal Reserve holds rates steady at its late-October meeting and helped equities rally while short-dated yields eased.
summary: September payrolls rose just 29,000 and unemployment climbed to 4.2%, boosting bets the Fed pauses in October.
context:
• The Fed has been in a tightening cycle, with the policy rate near 3.9% as it fights sticky inflation.

• Hiring has slowed through 2026, with the prior 12-month average monthly gain around 45,000.

• Markets have been torn between resilient activity and signs the jobs engine is cooling.
happened:
• Payrolls rose 29,000 in September versus forecasts near 84,000, with July and August revised down a combined 60,000.

• The jobless rate rose to 4.2% and labour-force participation edged up to 61.8%; the private sector added 46,000 jobs while government shed 17,000.

• Traders moved to price roughly a 77% chance the Fed holds in October, though a December hike is still seen as likely.
implications:
• A softer labour market gives the Fed room to pause even with inflation above target.

• Further weakness could shift the debate from rate hikes to the timing of eventual cuts.

• Upcoming September CPI and PPI releases will test whether the pause thesis holds.
importance:
• Payrolls are the week's pivotal macro catalyst, steering both the rates and equity narratives.

• A dovish repricing supports richly valued growth and technology names most exposed to rates.

• The downward revisions raise questions about the true underlying pace of US hiring.

title: Bond Rout Drives 30-Year Yield to 2002 High
content: The global bond sell-off deepened, with the 30-year US Treasury yield climbing above 5.6% to its highest level since 2002 and the 10-year holding near 5.28%. Inflation angst tied to elevated oil, heavy corporate and government debt supply and an unwind of the yen-funded carry trade combined to drive the biggest Treasury rout since the April 2025 tariff shock, keeping long-dated yields elevated even after a weak jobs report.
summary: The 30-year Treasury yield rose above 5.6% to a 2002 high as inflation fears and heavy supply fuelled a global bond rout.
context:
• Long-end yields have marched higher through 2026 on sticky inflation and fiscal-sustainability worries.

• Elevated oil prices tied to Middle East conflict have reinforced bets that central banks stay restrictive.

• An unwind of the yen carry trade has added a technical leg to the global sell-off.
happened:
• The 30-year yield pushed above 5.6% to touch its highest level since 2002.

• The 10-year yield held near 5.28% and the 2-year near 4.84%, with the curve steep at the long end.

• Yields rose even after the soft September payrolls print, underscoring supply and inflation pressures.
implications:
• Higher-for-longer long rates raise borrowing costs across mortgages, corporates and governments.

• Persistent long-end pressure caps valuations for rate-sensitive equities and lengthens the duration drag on portfolios.

• Relief hinges on oil cooling, lighter issuance or clearer signs of disinflation.
importance:
• Treasuries are the global risk-free benchmark, so the move reverberates across every asset class.

• A 2002-high long yield marks a structural shift in the cost of capital.

• The rout is now the dominant force dictating equity, FX and commodity direction.

title: Nasdaq Hits Record as Chips Lead Narrow Rally
content: US stocks rose on Friday after the soft jobs report, with the Nasdaq Composite climbing 1.2% to 27,190.86 and touching an intraday record as chip and software names led the advance. The S&P 500 gained 0.7% to 7,722.72 and the Dow added about 250 points, or 0.5%, to 51,176.46, but the rally was narrow: for the week the Nasdaq rose 0.5% while the S&P slipped 0.3% and the Dow fell 1.3%.
summary: The Nasdaq hit an intraday record and rose 1.2% on Friday as chips led a narrow rally, even as the Dow lagged for the week.
context:
• Megacap technology and AI-linked chipmakers have driven 2026's equity gains, concentrating market leadership.

• Higher Treasury yields have pressured the broader market, leaving rallies increasingly reliant on a few names.

• A soft jobs report revived hopes the Fed will pause, offering relief to rate-sensitive growth stocks.
happened:
• The Nasdaq Composite rose 1.2% (+319.27) to 27,190.86, hitting an intraday all-time high.

• The S&P 500 added 0.7% to 7,722.72 and the Dow gained about 250 points to 51,176.46.

• For the week the Nasdaq rose 0.5% while the S&P fell 0.3% and the Dow dropped 1.3%, with small caps lagging.
implications:
• Narrow leadership leaves indices vulnerable if AI and chip sentiment wobbles.

• A dovish Fed path would broaden participation beyond megacap technology.

• Any renewed spike in long-end yields is the clearest threat to richly valued growth names.
importance:
• Record highs sit atop a thin base, raising the stakes around a handful of leaders.

• The split between the Nasdaq and the Dow signals investors chasing growth over cyclicals.

• Market direction hinges on whether the rally broadens or stays concentrated.

title: European Stocks Rebound as Bond Rout Eases
content: European equities bounced on Friday after two days of losses, with Germany's DAX jumping 1.21% and the pan-European STOXX 600 adding 0.75% as a pause in the global bond sell-off offered relief. The STOXX 50 rose 0.3%, Britain's FTSE 100 gained 0.3% to 10,459.95 and the euro-zone EU50 benchmark climbed 1.14% to 6,247, though the index remained down about 2% over the past month.
summary: European shares rebounded on Friday, led by a 1.21% jump in the DAX, as a steadier bond market lifted sentiment.
context:
• European markets have outperformed earlier in 2026 on strong corporate earnings, leaving the EU50 up double digits year on year.

• The global bond sell-off had weighed on rate-sensitive sectors across the region.

• Elevated energy prices tied to Middle East conflict remain a headwind for European growth.
happened:
• The DAX rose 1.21% (+301.79) to 25,241.14 and the STOXX 600 added 0.75% to 631.34.

• The FTSE 100 gained 0.3% to 10,459.95 and the STOXX 50 rose 0.3%.

• The euro-zone EU50 climbed 1.14% to 6,247, trimming a monthly decline of about 2%.
implications:
• A calmer bond market is the key near-term support for European equities.

• Renewed yield pressure or higher oil would quickly test the rebound.

• Resilient earnings could keep drawing global investors toward relatively cheaper European names.
importance:
• Europe offers a valuation and diversification alternative to US megacap concentration.

• The rebound shows how tightly regional equities are now tracking the global rates story.

• The FTSE 100's grind near record territory reflects commodity and defensive exposure.

title: Hang Seng Slides as Asian Tech Stays Pressured
content: Asian equities were mixed to weaker on Friday, with Hong Kong's Hang Seng falling 2.6% to 23,972 as technology stocks stayed under pressure from higher global yields and US curbs on advanced AI hardware. Japan's Nikkei 225 eased 0.94% to 68,309 but remained up more than 6% on the month and close to records, leaving a wide divergence between buoyant Japanese shares and a sliding Hong Kong market.
summary: Hong Kong's Hang Seng fell 2.6% as tech stayed pressured, while Japan's Nikkei dipped but held near records.
context:
• Chinese and Hong Kong tech names have faced US restrictions on advanced AI hardware and soft sentiment.

• Japanese equities have surged in 2026, up nearly 50% year on year, aided by a weak yen.

• Rising global yields and geopolitical tension have weighed broadly on Asian risk appetite.
happened:
• The Hang Seng fell 2.6% to 23,972, down about 5% over the past month.

• The Nikkei 225 slipped 0.94% to 68,309 but held a monthly gain above 6%.

• Technology shares led declines amid higher yields and AI-hardware export curbs.
implications:
• Continued US export curbs keep a cloud over Chinese and Hong Kong technology valuations.

• A weaker yen keeps flattering Japanese exporter earnings but raises intervention risk.

• Divergence within Asia complicates broad regional allocation calls.
importance:
• Asia's split performance is a live test of the AI-hardware trade's geographic winners.

• Hong Kong weakness signals fragile confidence in China's growth and policy support.

• Japan's resilience ties directly to the yen and the global rates backdrop.

title: Yen Slips Past 158 After BoJ Underwhelms
content: The yen weakened beyond 158 per dollar before settling around 157.8 after the Bank of Japan's September summary of opinions fell short of investor hopes for stronger hawkish signals. The move reflects a widening policy gap with a still-restrictive Federal Reserve, and an unwind of yen-funded carry trades has been cited as one driver of the broader global bond sell-off.
summary: The yen slipped past 158 per dollar before steadying near 157.8 after the BoJ's September minutes disappointed hawks.
context:
• The BoJ has been cautiously normalising policy while signalling concern about inflation overshooting its target.

• A wide US-Japan rate differential has kept the yen under persistent pressure through 2026.

• Yen-funded carry trades have amplified moves across global bond and FX markets.
happened:
• USD/JPY touched beyond 158 before easing to about 157.83, down 0.15% on the day.

• The BoJ's September summary of opinions lacked the hawkish tilt some investors expected.

• EUR/JPY traded around 176.99 as the cross stayed elevated.
implications:
• Further yen weakness raises the risk of official intervention or firmer BoJ rhetoric.

• A disorderly carry-trade unwind could spill back into global bonds and equities.

• The currency's path hinges on the gap between Fed and BoJ policy expectations.
importance:
• USD/JPY is a key barometer of global rate differentials and risk appetite.

• Carry-trade dynamics link the yen directly to the worldwide bond rout.

• A weak yen supports Japanese exporters but imports inflation into Japan.

title: Bitcoin Holds Near $85K Before Fed Decision
content: Bitcoin held near $85,000 on Friday, opening around $84,850 and rising about 1.6% as crypto prices firmed ahead of the September jobs report. The token has gained roughly 44% over the past three months, but slowing spot-ETF inflows, elevated oil prices and uncertainty over the Federal Reserve's late-October meeting threaten to cap the rally as traders weigh the higher-yield backdrop.
summary: Bitcoin held near $85,000, up about 1.6% on the day, with the Fed's late-October decision looming as the key risk.
context:
• Bitcoin has rallied around 44% over three months, supported by spot-ETF demand.

• US spot bitcoin ETFs drew roughly $2.5bn of net inflows in the three weeks through 29 September, per Bitfinex.

• Rising Treasury yields and firm oil have tightened financial conditions for risk assets.
happened:
• Bitcoin opened around $84,850 on Friday, up about 1.6%, trading near $85,000.

• ETF inflows have shown signs of slowing even after a strong three-week stretch.

• Developers eye Bitcoin Core 32.0's release on 10 October and Ethereum's Glamsterdam testnet on 6 October.
implications:
• A hawkish Fed surprise in late October could unwind part of the summer rally.

• Sustained ETF inflows remain the key swing factor for near-term support.

• Higher yields and firm oil keep macro headwinds in play for digital assets.
importance:
• Bitcoin increasingly trades as a macro risk asset sensitive to the rates path.

• ETF flows have become a primary driver of marginal demand.

• The Fed's decision is a shared catalyst for crypto and traditional risk markets.

title: Micron's $54bn Quarter Supercharges AI Memory
content: Micron delivered a blowout fiscal fourth quarter, reporting revenue of $54.23bn — up 379% from a year earlier — as demand for AI-linked memory drove records in revenue, margin and earnings. Adjusted earnings of $33.42 a share beat the $31.61 expected, data-centre revenue jumped eleven-fold and management said favourable memory-market dynamics should persist for the next couple of years, reinforcing the AI-hardware trade leading equity indices.
summary: Micron reported $54.23bn in quarterly revenue, up 379%, as AI memory demand drove records and strong guidance.
context:
• An AI-driven supply crunch has sent prices for high-bandwidth memory (HBM) sharply higher.

• Micron shares have soared more than 500% over the past year on the memory boom.

• Memory is a bottlenecked part of the data-centre supply chain feeding AI workloads.
happened:
• Micron posted Q4 revenue of $54.23bn, up 379% year on year, versus $51.07bn expected.

• Adjusted EPS came in at $33.42 against the $31.61 consensus, with full-year revenue of $133.19bn, up 256%.

• Data-centre revenue jumped eleven-fold and HBM grew faster than overall sales.
implications:
• Durable memory pricing underpins earnings for the broader AI-hardware complex.

• Guidance for continued strength supports elevated chip-sector valuations.

• A demand or pricing wobble would hit the narrow leadership driving indices.
importance:
• Micron is a bellwether for the AI memory cycle powering the Nasdaq's records.

• The results validate the capital-spending surge across AI data centres.

• Chip earnings remain the single biggest swing factor for US equity leadership.
